title: Representation learning and self-supervision
html:
Part II · Advanced track · Session 7 of 10

Representation learning and self-supervision

Learning from unlabelled data: contrastive, non-contrastive, masked and predictive objectives.

Slides for this session

Starting point

Many records, few labels

A hospital holds follow-up records for tens of thousands of transplant recipients: doses, drug levels, laboratory values, reports.

Graft loss is recorded for a few thousand of them. Biopsy-proven rejection is annotated for a few hundred.

How can the unlabelled majority make the labelled minority sufficient?

Here is the usual situation in clinical research. Tens of thousands of patients with rich follow-up: doses, drug levels, laboratory values, reports. But the outcome you care about is available for a few thousand, and a carefully annotated one, such as biopsy-proven rejection, for a few hundred. Training a deep network on a few hundred labels fails. Yet the unlabelled records contain a great deal of structure: how creatinine evolves, how levels respond to dose changes. Self-supervised learning uses that structure to build an encoder first, so that a few hundred labels are enough afterwards.

Learning objectives

By the end of this session you will be able to:

  • Define a representation, and state what makes one good.
  • Write the InfoNCE loss and explain the role of the temperature.
  • Explain how non-contrastive, masked and predictive methods avoid collapse.
  • Choose views, masks and evaluation protocols for a modality that is not an image.

Four objectives. Define a representation and say what makes one good. Write the contrastive loss, InfoNCE, and explain what the temperature does. Explain how the other families, non-contrastive, masked, and predictive, avoid the trivial solution called collapse. And, most important for your own work, choose views, masks and evaluation protocols for data that are not natural images.

Outline

  1. What is a good representation?The pre-train, then adapt pipeline
  2. Contrastive learningInfoNCE, temperature, alignment and uniformity
  3. Learning without negativesSelf-distillation and explicit regularizers
  4. Masked and predictive objectivesMAE, JEPA, and contrastive pairs across modalities
  5. Views, evaluation, pitfallsThe augmentation question outside images

Five parts. What a representation is, and the pipeline it serves. Contrastive learning, in detail. Methods that work without negative pairs. Masked and predictive objectives, and contrastive learning across modalities. And finally the practical questions: which views, which evaluation, which pitfalls.

Pre-train once, adapt many times

The encoder is trained without labels; only a small head needs them.

raw record

images, sequences, molecules

Encoder f
pre-trained,
no labels

z = f(x)
representation

Small head

prediction

The representation z is the product. The pre-training objective is only a means to obtain it.

The pipeline has two stages. First, an encoder f is trained on unlabelled data with a self-supervised objective. This is the expensive step, and it is done once. The encoder maps a raw input x, an image, a sequence, a molecule, to a vector z of a few hundred numbers: the representation. Second, for each task, a small head is trained on top of z with the few labels available: a linear layer, or a small network. The same encoder serves many tasks: graft-loss prediction, rejection, phenotyping, retrieval of similar patients. Everything in this session is about the first stage.

What makes a representation good?

Three properties, in decreasing order of how easily they are measured.

Useful with a simple head

A linear classifier on z does well, with few labels. Information is not only present, it is easy to extract.

Invariant to nuisance, sensitive to signal

z should ignore the assay batch or the scanner, and keep the dose, the timing, the lesion. Deciding which is which is the whole difficulty.

Transferable

z still works on another hospital, another period, another task. This is the property clinicians need and the one papers test least.

What makes a representation good? Three properties. First, it is useful with a simple head: a linear classifier on top does well with few labels. The information is not only present, it is easy to extract. Second, it is invariant to nuisance factors and sensitive to signal. It should ignore the assay batch or the scanner model and keep the dose, the timing, the lesion. Deciding what is nuisance and what is signal is the whole difficulty, and we will return to it. Third, it transfers: to another hospital, another period, another task. This is what clinical use requires, and what papers test least.

Four families of self-supervised learning

They differ in the training signal and in how they avoid the trivial solution.

FamilyTraining signalHow collapse is avoidedExamples
ContrastiveViews of the same example match; views of different examples do notNegative pairsSimCLR, MoCo, CLIP
Non-contrastiveViews of the same example matchAsymmetry between branches, or explicit variance termsBYOL, DINO, VICReg
Masked modellingReconstruct hidden parts of the inputThe target is the data itselfBERT, MAE
Latent predictionPredict the representation of hidden partsSlowly moving target encoderI-JEPA

Four families. Contrastive methods say: two views of the same example should have similar representations, and views of different examples should not. Non-contrastive methods keep only the first half. That raises a problem: mapping every input to the same vector satisfies the objective perfectly. This is collapse, and each method has a mechanism against it. Masked modelling hides part of the input and reconstructs it; the target is the data, so collapse is not an issue. Latent prediction hides part of the input and predicts its representation rather than its raw values. Keep this table in mind; the rest of the session fills it in.

The contrastive principle

Two views of one example are a positive pair; everything else in the batch is a negative.

blue: two views of one patient, pulled together

black: other patients, pushed away

  • Build two views of each example: two crops of an image, two masked versions of a record.
  • Pull the two views together in embedding space.
  • Push the views of other examples away.
  • No label is used: the pairing comes from the data.

The contrastive principle. Take an example and build two views of it: two random crops of an image, or two differently masked versions of a patient record. Encode both. These two embeddings form a positive pair, in blue. All other embeddings in the batch come from other examples: they are negatives, in black. The loss pulls the positive pair together and pushes the negatives away. No label is used anywhere; the supervision is the knowledge of which views came from the same example. Everything the model learns is therefore determined by how you build the views.

The InfoNCE loss

A classification problem: find the positive among all candidates.

Reading the equation

Embeddings of the two views of the same example: the positive pair.

Cosine similarity: the dot product of the two vectors after normalizing them to length 1.

Sum over all other embeddings in the batch: the positive and 2N − 2 negatives, for a batch of N examples.

The temperature: a small positive number that sharpens the distribution.

Cross-entropy over candidates: the label is “which one is the other view of me?”

Here is the loss. Read it as a classification problem. For the anchor z i, there are two N minus one candidates in the batch: one positive, z j, and the rest negatives. We compute the cosine similarity of the anchor with each candidate, divide by a temperature tau, and apply a softmax. The loss is the negative log-probability assigned to the positive. It is the cross-entropy of session five, where the classes are the candidates. Minimizing it maximizes a lower bound on the mutual information between the two views, and that bound cannot exceed the logarithm of the number of candidates: one reason large batches help.

Try it

  • τ = 0.05: the positive gets 0.98, the hard negative 0.02. Only the hard negative produces gradient.
  • τ = 1: the positive gets only 0.30; all negatives count almost equally.
  • Small τ: sharper separation, but similar examples are torn apart.
  • Typical values: 0.05 to 0.2. Treat it as a hyperparameter of first importance.

The temperature is not a detail. Here are the softmax probabilities for one positive, with similarity zero point nine, and five negatives, for three temperatures. In blue, tau equals zero point zero five: the positive gets 0.98 and almost all the rest goes to the hardest negative, the one with similarity zero point seven. The gradient comes from hard negatives only. In grey, tau equals one: the distribution is nearly flat, the positive gets 0.30, and every negative counts about the same. A low temperature separates fine-grained differences, but it also pushes apart examples that truly are similar, two patients with the same phenotype for instance. Typical values lie between zero point zero five and zero point two.

Alignment and uniformity

What the contrastive loss optimizes, split in two.

Reading the equation

The embedding, normalized to length 1: a point on a sphere.

A positive pair. Alignment: positives should be close.

Two independent examples. Uniformity: embeddings should spread over the whole sphere.

collapsed

aligned and uniform

Collapse satisfies alignment and fails uniformity.

A useful way to understand the contrastive loss, due to Wang and Isola. It does two things. Alignment: the two views of an example should land close to each other; the first line is their mean squared distance. Uniformity: embeddings of different examples should spread evenly over the sphere; the second line is small when points are far apart. On the left, a collapsed representation: perfectly aligned, not uniform at all, and useless. On the right, what we want. These two numbers can be computed on any encoder and are good diagnostics during pre-training, long before you have a downstream result.

Learning without negatives

Each method replaces negatives by another mechanism against collapse.

MethodMechanism against collapseRemark
BYOL, SimSiamA predictor on one branch and a stop-gradient on the other; in BYOL the target is a moving average of the online networkWorks with small batches
DINO, DINOv2The teacher is a moving average of the student; its outputs are centred and sharpenedStrong general-purpose image features
Barlow TwinsThe cross-correlation matrix between the two views is driven to the identityDecorrelates the dimensions
VICRegExplicit variance, invariance and covariance termsThe most transparent objective

Negatives have a cost: large batches, and the risk of pushing apart examples that are truly similar. Can we do without them? Yes, with care. BYOL and SimSiam make the two branches asymmetric: one has an extra predictor, and the gradient is stopped on the other. In BYOL the target branch is a slowly moving average of the online one. DINO uses a moving-average teacher and centres and sharpens its outputs; DINOv2 is today a standard source of image features. Barlow Twins makes the cross-correlation matrix of the two views close to the identity. VICReg, on the next slide, writes each requirement as an explicit term.

VICReg: each requirement as one term

The clearest statement of what a joint-embedding method needs.

Reading the equation

The batch of embeddings for the first and second views.

Invariance: mean squared distance between the two views of each example.

Variance: keeps the standard deviation of every dimension, across the batch, above a threshold. This term forbids collapse.

Covariance: penalizes correlations between dimensions, so that they carry different information.

Invariance alone collapses. Variance prevents it. Covariance spreads information across dimensions.

VICReg is worth knowing because it states the requirements one by one. Z and Z prime are the embeddings of the two views for a whole batch. The first term, s, is invariance: the two views of each example should match. Alone, it leads to collapse. The second term, v, is variance: each dimension of the embedding must keep a standard deviation above a threshold across the batch. A constant embedding has zero variance, so this term forbids collapse. The third term, c, penalizes covariance between dimensions, so that the dimensions do not all encode the same thing. This last failure, where the embedding uses only a few directions, is called dimensional collapse.

Masked modelling

Hide most of the input, reconstruct it.

Reading the equation

The set of masked positions: 75 % of patches in MAE, 15 % of tokens in BERT.

The encoder; it sees only the visible part.

A light decoder, discarded after pre-training.

Encoder
visible only

Decoder

75 % hidden

reconstruction

input patches

we keep this

The mask ratio sets the difficulty: high for redundant signals, low for dense ones.

The second large family: masked modelling. Hide a random set M of positions; the encoder sees only the visible part; a light decoder predicts the hidden values; the loss is the reconstruction error on the masked positions. For categorical tokens, replace the squared error by a cross-entropy: that is BERT. The decoder is thrown away afterwards; we keep the encoder. One parameter matters: the mask ratio. Images are highly redundant, so the masked autoencoder hides seventy-five percent of the patches, otherwise the task is solved by local interpolation. Text is dense, so BERT hides fifteen percent. For a new modality, ask how redundant it is.

Predicting in latent space: JEPA

Predict the representation of the hidden part, not its raw values.

context
(visible part)

target
(hidden part)

Context
encoder

Target encoder
moving average

Predictor

loss in latent space

slow copy

no pixel or value is reconstructed

  • A context encoder reads the visible part.
  • A target encoder, a moving average of the first, reads the hidden part.
  • A predictor maps one representation to the other; the loss is computed between representations.
  • Unpredictable detail, such as measurement noise, does not have to be modelled.

A more recent idea: joint-embedding predictive architectures. Masked autoencoders reconstruct raw values, so they spend capacity on details that may be pure noise. Here the context encoder reads the visible part; a target encoder, which is a slowly moving average of the context encoder, reads the hidden part; and a predictor maps the context representation to the target representation. The loss is computed between representations. Nothing is reconstructed in input space. The attraction for clinical measurements is clear: assay noise and irrelevant fluctuation do not need to be predicted. Collapse is avoided by the moving-average target, as in BYOL.

Contrastive learning across modalities

The two “views” are two modalities of the same object.

Reading the equation

Normalized embeddings of the i-th image and of its text, from two separate encoders.

The batch size: each image must pick its own caption among N.

The full loss averages both directions, image to text and text to image (CLIP). After training, a class can be described in words and recognized without any labelled example: zero-shot classification.

The views do not have to come from augmentation. They can be two modalities of the same object: an image and its caption, a chest radiograph and its report, a molecule and the description of its assay. This is CLIP. Two encoders, one per modality. For a batch of N pairs, each image must find its own text among the N texts, and each text its own image. It is the InfoNCE loss, with a different notion of positive pair. After training, the two modalities live in one space. You can then classify an image by comparing it with the embeddings of sentences describing each class, with no labelled image: zero-shot classification. We return to multimodal fusion in session ten.

The augmentation question

A view states an invariance. A wrong invariance deletes the signal.

ModalityCommon views or masksWhat to question
ImagesCrops, colour jitter, blurIn histology, colour carries diagnostic information
MoleculesSMILES enumeration, atom masking, conformersA small structural edit can change activity completely
ProteinsMasking residuesOne mutation can abolish function
Clinical sequencesMasking events, time windows, dropping a modalityTime since the last dose and dose size are signal, not nuisance

Before choosing an augmentation, ask: would a pharmacologist call these two inputs equivalent?

This is the slide I would like you to remember. A view is a statement: these two inputs should have the same representation. In other words, an invariance. If the invariance is wrong, the encoder is trained to delete signal. Colour jitter is harmless for photographs of dogs; in histology, stain colour is diagnostic. For molecules, a small edit can change activity by orders of magnitude: so-called activity cliffs. For clinical sequences, shifting timestamps or rescaling doses would make the encoder blind to exactly what pharmacology is about. Masking and predictive objectives are often safer than augmentation here, because they assume less.

Evaluating a representation

Report several protocols; each answers a different question.

ProtocolWhat is trainedWhat it tells you
Linear probeA linear layer on frozen featuresWhether the information is easy to extract
k-nearest neighboursNothingThe geometry of the space, without hyperparameters
Fine-tuningThe whole networkThe best achievable performance
Label-efficiency curveHead or whole network, with 1 %, 10 %, 100 % of labelsThe practical value of pre-training
Transfer under shiftEvaluated on another site or periodRobustness: what clinical use requires

How do you know the representation is good? Not by the pre-training loss, which is not comparable across methods. Use downstream protocols, and report several. A linear probe: freeze the encoder, train a linear layer. It tells you whether information is easy to extract. Nearest neighbours: no training at all. Fine-tuning gives the best achievable number but hides the quality of the representation. The label-efficiency curve, performance with one, ten and a hundred percent of the labels, shows the practical value of pre-training. And transfer under shift, to another site or period, is what clinical use requires.

  • With many labels, pre-training and training from scratch often converge.
  • With few labels, the pre-trained encoder is far ahead.
  • The gain is largest exactly where clinical datasets live: hundreds to thousands of labelled patients.
  • Always include a strong non-deep baseline on the same splits.

What should you expect? This schematic shows the typical shape; it is not measured data. On the horizontal axis, the number of labelled examples, on a logarithmic scale. With tens of thousands of labels, training from scratch catches up with the pre-trained encoder. With a few hundred, the pre-trained encoder is far ahead. The gain is largest exactly where clinical datasets live. One caution: always include a strong non-deep baseline on the same splits, boosted trees on hand-crafted summaries for instance. On small tabular problems it often remains the model to beat.

InfoNCE in eleven lines

The SimCLR loss for a batch of N pairs.

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def info_nce(z1, z2, tau=0.2):
    # z1, z2: (N, d) embeddings of two views
    z = F.normalize(torch.cat([z1, z2]), dim=1)
    sim = z @ z.T / tau                # (2N, 2N) logits
    sim.fill_diagonal_(float("-inf"))  # no self-pairs
    N = z1.shape[0]
    pos = torch.arange(2 * N).roll(N)  # the positive
    return F.cross_entropy(sim, pos)
  • normalize: dot products become cosine similarities.
  • The diagonal is set to −∞: an embedding is not its own candidate.
  • pos: for row i the positive sits N positions away.
  • The loss is an ordinary cross-entropy over 2N − 1 candidates.

The loss as code. z one and z two hold the embeddings of the two views for a batch of N examples. We concatenate and normalize them, so that dot products are cosine similarities. The similarity matrix, divided by the temperature, is two N by two N. We set the diagonal to minus infinity, because an embedding is not a candidate for itself. For row i, the positive is the other view of the same example, which sits N rows away; that is what the roll computes. Then a plain cross-entropy. Eleven lines. The difficulty of contrastive learning is not the loss; it is the choice of views.

Your turn

A loss by hand, and four candidate views

  1. For one anchor, the cosine similarities are: positive 0.8; negatives 0.2, 0.0 and −0.4. Compute the InfoNCE loss with τ = 0.2, then with τ = 1.
  2. You pre-train on tacrolimus monitoring sequences: dose, trough level, creatinine, time. For each candidate view, is the implied invariance sensible?
  3. (a) Masking 30 % of the events. (b) Shifting all times by a random offset of up to 12 hours.
  4. (c) Multiplying all doses by a random factor. (d) Dropping all creatinine values.

Time: 10 minutes · Material: A calculator with exp and ln · Deliverable: Two losses; four verdicts with one line of justification each

Show the solution
  • τ = 0.2: logits 4, 1, 0, −2; exponentials 54.6, 2.72, 1, 0.14; p = 0.934; loss = 0.068. τ = 1: p = 0.435; loss = 0.833.
  • (a) Sensible. Hidden events can be inferred from the rest; this is masked modelling.
  • (b) Not sensible. Twelve hours turns a trough into a peak: timing is the signal.
  • (c) Not sensible. The dose–exposure relation is what the encoder should learn. (d) Sensible, as robustness to a missing modality.

Time and dose are signal. Any view that hides them teaches the encoder to ignore pharmacology.

Solutions. With temperature zero point two, the logits are four, one, zero and minus two. The exponentials are 54.6, 2.72, one and 0.14. The positive gets probability 0.934 and the loss is 0.068. With temperature one, the probability falls to 0.435 and the loss rises to 0.833: the same embeddings, a very different loss. For the views. Masking events is sensible. Shifting times by up to twelve hours is not: with twice-daily dosing it turns a trough into a peak. Rescaling doses is not: the relation between dose and exposure is precisely what we want the encoder to capture. Dropping creatinine is sensible, as robustness to a missing modality.

Self-check

One correct answer per question.

1. In InfoNCE, lowering the temperature:

The softmax sharpens, so the most similar negatives dominate.

2. A collapsed representation is:

All inputs map to the same point: positives coincide, and so does everything else.

3. Masked autoencoders hide 75 % of image patches because:

With little masking, neighbouring patches make the task trivial.

Key takeaways

  1. Self-supervision turns unlabelled data into an encoder; a small head then needs few labels.
  2. Contrastive learning = alignment of positives + uniformity of everything; the temperature controls the balance.
  3. Without negatives, collapse must be prevented by asymmetry or by explicit variance terms.
  4. Masked and latent-prediction objectives assume less than augmentation: often safer for clinical and molecular data.
  5. A view is an invariance. Time and dose are signal.

Five takeaways. Self-supervision turns unlabelled data into an encoder, and a small head then needs few labels. Contrastive learning is alignment of positives plus uniformity of everything, with the temperature controlling the balance. Without negatives, collapse must be prevented by asymmetry or explicit variance terms. Masked and latent-prediction objectives assume less than augmentation and are often safer for clinical and molecular data. And a view is an invariance: time and dose are signal.
